items.title: Years after NEP spoke of digital literacy, 3 of 4 govt schools still don’t have a functional desktop
items.summary: In May 2020, as India was preparing to overhaul its education policy, the Narendra Modi government held a review meeting on education that placed technology at the centre, to help build what the government described as a “global knowledge super power”. Two months later, the Union Cabinet approved the National Education Policy. It made digital literacy, coding and computational thinking essential skills for every student. Coding activities were proposed to begin in the middle stage (Grades 6–8), while mathematics and computational thinking had to receive stronger focus from the foundational years. In September that year, PM Modi spoke about what education should look like in the 21st century – from coding to artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, cloud computing, data science and robotics. But five years later, the latest 2025-26 UDISE+ (Unified District Information System for Education Plus) data presents a stark picture on digital awareness inside India’s schools. UDISE+ describes itself as the Ministry of Education’s official school education information system and says its data is collected from recognised schools and validated through administrative levels. items.title: Allahabad High Court takes serious note of IAS officer's alleged attempt to influence trial judge
items.summary: The Allahabad High Court recently expressed concern over allegations that senior Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer Durga Shakti Nagpal had attempted to pressure a trial judge through a phone call in connection with a long-pending land case [ Jyoti Vidya Mandir v Nagar Palika Parishad & Ors. ]. In a letter to the district judge, the civil judge alleged that the IAS officer attempted to exert pressure on her during a phone conversation by questioning her about her leave and seeking to discuss a pending case. The IAS officer has maintained that she had not tried to discuss the merits of the case, and had only sought to know when the judge would resume hearing the matter. On August 21, Justice Syed Qamar Hasan Rizvi of the High Court took a serious view of the allegations against the IAS officer. "The tone and language of the aforesaid alleged telephonic conversation given a direct impression that the Presiding Officer of the Court was tried to be influenced and that made her feel offended ... It is shocking that how a litigating party can approach the Court by making such a phone call and that too in context with a pending matter before the said Court ," observed the Court.

items.title: Karnataka High Court stays proceedings against man accused of ghosting, seen-zoning his partner
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently stayed criminal proceedings against a man accused of sex on the false promise of marriage after ghosting and 'seen-zoning' his partner [Thufail Ahmed v. State] . Justice M Nagaprasanna observed that the petitioner's conduct did not fulfil the ingredients of Section 69 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023. "It is the allegation that the petitioner had begun to seenzone the respondent and ghost her throughout. Therefore, the offence under s.69 has sprung. Except this there is nothing else that could become the ingredients of the offence under s.69. In that light there shall be an interim order of stay on further proceedings qua the petitioner till the next date of hearing." Justice M Nagaprasanna Both parties were in a relationship since December 2025. The petitioner told his then partner that he was visiting Chennai, where ailing father was undergoing treatment. The ex-partner, suspecting that the petitioner had told her a lie, asked him to receive her video call. The petitioner refused to receive calls and eventually blocked her. The woman then filed a complaint alleging that the petitioner had committed offences of Section 69 and 115, BNS .

items.title: Tarun Tejpal should have surrendered before challenging rape conviction: Goa tells Supreme Court
items.summary: The Goa government on Monday told the Supreme Court that former Tehelka editor Tarun Tejpal, convicted in rape case, should should have surrendered before filing an appeal challenging his conviction before the top court. Tejpal's appeal was listed before Justice Alok Aradhe today, in the chamber list in which matters are sometimes taken up for preliminary or procedural considerations before it is listed before a regular Bench. Justice Alok Aradhe Representing the Goa government, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta submitted, "Existence of the appeal is dependent on either filing a certificate that he has surrendered or, alternatively, he will have to pray to Your Lordships to allow an exemption from surrendering. These are the two options. My respectful submission is, look at the seriousness of the matter." Tushar Mehta Representing Tejpal, Senior Advocate Kapil Sibal countered that there was no need to surrender yet since the High Court itself had granted Tejpal time to surrender. items.title: Can contractual clauses mandate pre-deposit before arbitration? Supreme Court refers issue to larger bench
items.summary: The Supreme Court has doubted the correctness of its own ruling upholding arbitration clauses that require only contractors to deposit a percentage of their claim before invoking arbitration [Santosh Associate v. HSIIDC]. A Bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Manmohan asked the Chief Justice of India to consider referring the issue to a larger bench. Justice Manmohan and Justice Manoj Misra Accordingly, the Bench requested the Chief Justice of India to consider referring a set of questions to a larger bench. These include: • Whether a clause requiring only the contractor to make a pre-deposit before arbitration violates Section 18 of the Arbitration Act, which mandates equal treatment of both parties at every stage of arbitration. • Whether pre-deposit conditions discourage parties from turning to arbitration in the first place, defeating its purpose of easing the burden on courts. • Whether such a condition is arbitrary and violates the right to sue, Article 14 of the Constitution and Section 28 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. • Whether requiring a pre-deposit has any real connection to the goal of weeding out frivolous claims, given that frivolous claims can already be addressed
